TD versus Monte Carlo

Both methods learn the random walk from Lesson 45. With the step sizes S&B compare, every TD curve ends below every Monte Carlo curve. The reason is a trade: Monte Carlo's target is right on average but noisy, and TD's target is wrong at first but much calmer.

The race

The maths

Write $T$ for a target and $v = v_\pi(s)$ for the true value. A target's error splits into a systematic part and a random part:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[(T - v)^2\big] = \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}[T] - v\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[(T - \mathbb{E}[T])^2\big]}_{\text{variance}}$$

A target can be off because it aims at the wrong place, or because it scatters.

The Monte Carlo target is unbiased, because $v_\pi(s)$ is defined as its mean:

$$\mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid S_t = s] = v_\pi(s)$$

But $G_t$ depends on every random step to the end of the episode. In the random walk it is $0$ or $1$, so from C its variance is $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = 0.25$.

The TD target is unbiased only once the estimates are right:

$$\mathbb{E}_\pi\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s\big] - v_\pi(s) = \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_\pi\big[V(S_{t+1}) - v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s\big]$$

Its bias is the error in the next state's estimate. Its randomness comes from one step only. From C with true estimates the target is $\tfrac13$ or $\tfrac23$, with variance $(\tfrac16)^2 = \tfrac1{36} \approx 0.028$, nine times less than Monte Carlo.

As learning proceeds, TD's bias shrinks along with the estimates, while Monte Carlo's variance stays. That is why TD wins the race here. S&B §6.2 notes that nobody has proved TD always converges faster than Monte Carlo; in practice it usually does on stochastic tasks like this one.

With a constant $\alpha$ neither method settles exactly. The estimates keep chasing noisy targets, so the error levels off higher for larger $\alpha$. For TD with large $\alpha$ the curve even rises slightly after its early dip (S&B Exercise 6.5 asks why).
